title: India Opened the Door to Chinese Investment. Its Electronics Giants Walked the Other Way.
excerpt: Four months after New Delhi eased Press Note 3 to fast-track Chinese capital, India's biggest contract manufacturers have signed at least eight new partnerships — almost all with Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea.
body:
In March 2026, India's Union Cabinet did something it had resisted for six years: it eased Press Note 3, the foreign direct investment rule that had subjected all investment proposals from land-bordering countries — read: China — to case-by-case security clearance since the deadly 2020 Galwan Valley border clashes.

The revised policy, called Press Note 2, 2026, promised a 60-day fast-track approval window for Chinese-linked capital in seven strategic sectors, including electronic components, electronic capital goods, and rare-earth processing — precisely the categories India's contract manufacturers depend on most.

Four months later, the on-ground behavior of those very manufacturers tells a more cautious story than the policy announcement suggested.

Eight Deals, Almost None With China

Since March, companies including Dixon Technologies, Amber Enterprises, PG Electroplast, Epack Durable, and Syrma SGS Technology have signed or begun operating at least eight new manufacturing partnerships. Almost every single one is with a partner from Taiwan, Japan, or South Korea — not China.

Dixon Technologies, India's largest contract electronics manufacturer, is finalizing a joint venture with Taiwan's Inventec Corporation to produce laptops, servers, and desktops. Dixon holds 60% and Inventec 40% in the new entity, Dixon IT Devices Private Limited, which has already onboarded four of the world's top five global laptop brands. Separately, Dixon signed a binding term sheet with Taiwan's Gemtek Technology for telecom equipment manufacturing.

Syrma SGS Technology has partnered with Japan's Kaga Electronics to build a new plant serving Japanese customers. Epack Durable is operationalizing a joint venture with South Korea's Bumjin Electronics for smart audio devices. And Amber Enterprises broke ground last week on a printed circuit board plant with South Korea's Korea Circuit Co.

Even PG Electroplast, which had spent over 18 months pursuing a technical alliance with China's Highly Group for compressor manufacturing, ultimately abandoned the effort after prolonged regulatory hurdles and committed over ₹300 crore to build the facility independently.

The One Exception — Still Waiting

The reform's own test case remains the Dixon-Vivo joint venture, which would combine Dixon's PLI-backed manufacturing muscle with Chinese smartphone giant Vivo's brand reach. The proposal has cleared an inter-ministerial panel but is still awaiting the final government approval letter.

If it goes through, it would be among the most significant post-reform Chinese investments in Indian electronics. Dixon's mobile and EMS segment alone generated revenues of ₹44,257 crore in FY26, and the partnership is designed to boost domestic value addition and expand capacity for third-party OEM production.

Why Companies Are Hedging

Industry executives point to several reasons why the open door hasn't translated into a rush of Chinese deals. The regulatory overhang hasn't fully lifted — the 60-day window is an improvement, but approvals for Chinese-linked capital still require government scrutiny, and outcomes remain unpredictable. Supply chain diversification has become a boardroom mantra, with Dixon's managing director Atul Lall publicly framing the company's strategy as a way to "derisk and cut its complete dependence on China."

There's also the political calculus. Despite the border détente and Modi's visit to Beijing last August, anti-China sentiment remains potent in India's business and media environment. Companies seen as too close to Chinese partners face public scrutiny and investor questions.

Yet the cost-competitiveness gap is real. Chinese manufacturers maintain significant advantages in scale, technology, and production costs, particularly in mobile phones and home appliances. Replacing them with Taiwan or Japanese partners is technically feasible but rarely cheaper.

The Bigger Picture

India's electronics manufacturing sector is at an inflection point. The country wants to be a global electronics hub, and its PLI schemes have attracted real capital and scale. But the question of where technology and components come from — China, Taiwan, Japan, or homegrown — remains politically fraught and commercially consequential.

The pattern emerging from the post-reform period suggests Indian industry is reading the room: use the eased rules when Chinese technology is genuinely irreplaceable (as in Tata Motors' Chery EV platform deal), but default to non-Chinese partners for everything else.

For NRI investors and tech professionals watching India's manufacturing story, the message is clear: the "Make in India" supply chain is being built, but it's being built with a deliberate tilt toward democracies that share New Delhi's strategic alignment — even when Beijing's money and technology are finally being offered at the door.
